clue.text: Humble home address associated with song mainly

definitions.text: Humble home address associated with song mainly

parts.words: Humble home address associated with song mainly
parts.note: a district of poor huts, its first part also the name of a sailors' work song, a song of the main or open sea

explanation.surface: Someone describes a modest dwelling, its address, and a song linked with it.
explanation.walkthrough: A shanty is both a crude hut and a sea song; 'mainly' is a pun on the main, the open sea, where such songs were sung.
explanation.definitionFit: A settlement of makeshift huts on a city's edge is where the poorest people make their homes.

clue.text: Breaks for a game of cards on board

indicators.note: on board means aboard, so the card game goes inside the letters for a ship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, the vessel boarded
nap is a card game, short for Napoleon

explanation.surface: Sailors take breaks for a game of cards aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' is the standard device of putting something inside SS, the steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: To snap is to break suddenly, so snaps means breaks.

clue.text: But falls into and low price" (T Night)

definitions.text: But falls into and low price" (T Night)

parts.words: But falls into and low price" (T Night)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank line from Orsino's opening speech in Twelfth Night about love's appetite

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap, from Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
explanation.walkthrough: Orsino says whatever enters love's sea 'falls into abatement and low price, even in a minute'. T Night is Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means a lessening or decline in value, matching 'low price'.

clue.text: Batrachian 23 and road-hog badgered to reform

definitions.text: Batrachian 23 and road-hog badgered to reform

parts.words: Batrachian 23 and road-hog badgered to reform
parts.note: a wealthy amphibian motoring menace who is pressed by his friend Badger to mend his ways

explanation.surface: A rich frog-like speed merchant is nagged into changing his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Wind in the Willows the rich Toad (23 is MONEYBAGS) crashes motor cars and Badger tries to reform him; 'badgered' is a pun on Badger.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Grahame's character is a toad, an amphibian, rich and obsessed with fast cars.

clue.text: Comparatively tawdry row about a race

indicators.note: the word for row is placed about the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A row about a race grows more tawdry.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT is the Tourist Trophy, the Isle of Man motorcycle race; 'about' does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatty means shabby or cheap-looking, so this is its comparative form.

clue.text: Factory dance 'eld in Notts

parts.note: works means a factory, as in gasworks

indicators.note: the word held with its first letter dropped shows a dance word whose leading aitch is dropped too

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: A factory dance is held in Nottinghamshire, in local dialect.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped H in ''eld' tells you to drop the H of HOP, giving 'OP. Notts is short for Nottinghamshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: The market town lies in the north of Nottinghamshire, so it is a place found in that county.

clue.text: 500 for you once ?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed '500 for you once ?(4)'; THOU means 'you' formerly, but slang thou is a thousand, not 500, so the first half fits nothing

clue.text: Meeting place of a weird sorority

definitions.text: Meeting place of a weird sorority

parts.words: Meeting place of a weird sorority
parts.note: the Weird Sisters of Macbeth gather on open wasteland to meet Macbeth

explanation.surface: Where a strange sisterhood holds its gatherings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weird' means fate-wielding here: the Weird Sisters are Macbeth's three witches, who meet him on a blasted moor.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's witches meet Macbeth on open scrubland, the setting of their famous scene.

clue.text: Dig up lovely borders-out of this world

parts.note: to unearth is to dig up

indicators.note: the borders of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Digging up lovely flowerbeds is a heavenly pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'borders' looks like garden beds after 'dig up', but means the first and last letters of 'lovely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unearthly means supernatural or eerie, belonging to no earthly realm.

clue.text: Walpole's Gothic style shown here, oddly, by war thrillers

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, so the letters are arranged strangely

explanation.surface: Horace Walpole's Gothic manner seen, strangely, in war thrillers.
explanation.walkthrough: Horace Walpole built a Gothic Revival villa at Twickenham, giving its name to a style; 'oddly' rearranges BY WAR THRILLERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Walpole's Twickenham villa gave its name to the early Gothic Revival style he pioneered there.

clue.text: Robert, architect, worker in hard stone

parts.note: Robert Adam was an eighteenth-century Scottish architect
the worker ant is the crossword's stock worker

explanation.surface: A tribute to the architect Robert Adam as a craftsman carving hard stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamant was the legendary unbreakable stone, later used of diamond or any very hard mineral.

clue.text: Won by Samuel by more than one whisker?

definitions.text: Won by Samuel by more than one whisker?

parts.words: Won by Samuel by more than one whisker?
parts.note: Samuel Whiskers is the rodent villain of a Beatrix Potter tale, so a contest he wins is one among his kind, and the photo-finish phrase 'by a whisker' fits

explanation.surface: A close-run contest won by someone called Samuel by a narrow margin.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Whiskers is a rat in Beatrix Potter's stories; the clue imagines a literal race among rats and plays on winning 'by a whisker'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the fierce competitive struggle of working life, pictured as rodents scurrying in a contest.

clue.text: New format to issue unto Caesar's biographer

indicators.note: giving the words a new format means rearranging their letters into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Instructions to publish a work, newly formatted, for Caesar's biographer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New format' rearranges ISSUE UNTO; 'to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman historian wrote The Twelve Caesars, lives of Julius Caesar and the first emperors.

clue.text: Age. I do thee" (Shakespeare)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from The Passionate Pilgrim, which pairs hating age with adoring youth

explanation.surface: A quotation with a missing word, attributed to Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is 'Age, I do abhor thee; youth, I do adore thee', from The Passionate Pilgrim, published under Shakespeare's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to loathe, the opposite of adoring youth in the next phrase.

clue.text: Whence Roland bore good news

parts.note: in Browning's poem the horse Roland carries the good news from a Flemish city to Aix

explanation.surface: A question of where a messenger named Roland set out with good tidings.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem 'How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix' has the horse Roland finishing the ride; 'Roland' looks like the paladin of the Chanson de Roland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Flemish city is the starting point of the ride in Browning's poem, so it is where the news came from.

clue.text: Dinner with the ungodly-so indecorous

definitions.meaning: a meal among heathens, at which no blessing is said before eating

explanation.surface: Eating with heathens is such an unseemly business.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is cryptic: grace is the prayer before a meal, and the ungodly would skip it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both without a mealtime prayer and lacking elegance or good manners.

clue.text: Make new edition without local flavour

indicators.note: in the old sense of outside, the word for flavour sits outside and encloses the other piece

parts.note: relish is a flavour or taste
a local is a British name for one's neighbourhood pub

explanation.surface: Bring out a new edition of a cookbook with the regional flavour taken away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means outside here, not lacking. A local is a British name for your nearest pub.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring out a book again in a fresh printing is to issue it once more.

clue.text: Mimicking one upset musical little boy

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the words upside down, so they read from the bottom up

parts.note: Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical
Tim is a boy's name, short and so little

explanation.surface: One copycat puts a little boy off music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses the musical and the boy together, giving MITATIVE; in a down clue upset means read bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Copying the manner of another is imitation, so the adjective describes mimicry.

clue.text: Look hack in a genuine case for such calculation of risk

indicators.note: the turned piece goes in, sitting inside the word for genuine

parts.note: actual means genuine or real

indicators.note: look back asks for the word for look to be read in the backward direction

parts.note: air is a look or appearance, as in an air of mystery

explanation.surface: Someone glances back at an authentic case when working out insurance risks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the look word round to RIA, which goes 'in'; 'a' and 'case' are link words framing the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Actuaries are the insurance statisticians who compute risks and premiums, so their sums are of this kind.

clue.text: I am myself three quarters of maximum size

parts.note: contracted to I'm
me stands for myself
north, south and east are three of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone claims to be three-quarters of the largest possible size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three quarters' is three compass points, N, S and E, not a fraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Immense means vast, as large as can be.

clue.text: Bang on the forehead — so crazy!

definitions.text: Bang on the forehead — so crazy!

parts.words: Bang on the forehead — so crazy!
parts.note: tapping one's temple is the gesture for someone mad, and the word itself goes back to being moonstruck

explanation.surface: Someone knocks their head and exclaims how mad it all is.
explanation.definitionFit: A madman, once thought to be affected by the moon, is the person signalled by tapping the forehead.

clue.text: Some sunshine around at home ? Not this day

indicators.note: the word for some sunshine goes around the phrase for at home

parts.note: a ray is a single beam, some of the sunshine
in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: A ray of sunshine around the house, but not on a day like this.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: a day with wet weather is not one of sunshine.
explanation.definitionFit: A day of showers and wet weather is the opposite of a sunny one.

clue.text: OT character translated after 365 years

parts.note: Genesis gives this patriarch 365 years before God took him, and Hebrews says he was translated, carried bodily to heaven

explanation.surface: An Old Testament figure whose words were translated after a very long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' looks like a rendering into another language; in the biblical sense it means taken up to heaven without dying.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament patriarch walked with God 365 years and was then taken up, never dying.

clue.text: Nothing right about the alternative

indicators.note: the letters for nothing and right are placed about the article

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: Nothing is quite right about the other choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts O and R around THE.
explanation.definitionFit: The other one means the second or alternative choice.

clue.text: Being wealthy, there's one wearing my trousers

indicators.note: the number goes in the middle of my, as a body sits inside clothes worn

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
bags is old British slang for loose trousers, as in Oxford bags

explanation.surface: A rich man boasts that someone else is wearing his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' sets ONE in MY; bags are wide trousers in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich person is jokingly called by the name of sacks of cash, so 'being' is a noun here: a wealthy creature.

clue.text: In which priests piously perambulate

indicators.note: in tells you the answer lies inside the run of words that follows, spanning their joins

explanation.surface: A place where priests walk devoutly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: priests do walk in this covered cathedral passage, and it sits in 'prieStS piousLY PErambulate'.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word names a covered walkway in a cathedral or monastery, used by clergy.

clue.text: Troops stepped out in this formation

definitions.text: Troops stepped out in this formation

parts.words: Troops stepped out in this formation
parts.note: a military arrangement in which units stand in parallel lines each offset like the steps of a ladder

explanation.surface: Soldiers marching out in a particular parade arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stepped out' sounds like marching, but means arranged in steps, each unit staggered from the one beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived military term names a staggered, step-like arrangement of troops, ships or aircraft.

clue.text: A term at Oxford or Cambridge

definitions.text: A term at Oxford or Cambridge

parts.words: A term at Oxford or Cambridge
parts.note: the name of the Oxford summer term and of a large Cambridge college

explanation.surface: A question about the university calendar at Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford it names the summer term; at Cambridge it is one of the biggest colleges, so 'term' also reads as a word or name used there.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine of the threefold God gives its name to Oxford's summer term and to colleges at both universities.

clue.text: Costume Cleopatra's attendant returned

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the attendant's name is read from end to start

parts.note: Iras is one of Cleopatra's waiting-women in Antony and Cleopatra

explanation.surface: The costume of Cleopatra's maid has been sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: Iras, Cleopatra's maid in Shakespeare's play, read backwards gives the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: The draped garment is the national dress of Indian women, a kind of costume.

clue.text: " Queue knowledge" its warden might have called it

definitions.text: " Queue knowledge" its warden might have called it

indicators.text: its warden might have called it
indicators.note: the warden meant is the Oxford head famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the quoted phrase is his slip

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A college head with a habit of verbal slips might call his institution this.
explanation.walkthrough: William Spooner, whose name gave us the Spoonerism, was warden of New College, Oxford; swapping the first sounds of 'new col-' gives 'queue knowl-'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford college was headed by Spooner, so its warden is the one who would mangle its name this way.
